subtopics.title: Types of Errors in Mule 4
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how Mule 4's structured Error object and namespaced error types like HTTP:NOT_FOUND and MULE:CONNECTIVITY work, replacing Mule 3's exceptions entirely.
subtopics.summary: An overview of the Mule 4 Error object and the namespaced error type system used across core and connector errors.
subtopics.content_html:
Every Mule 4 application eventually has to deal with things going wrong: a downstream API times out, a database connection drops, or an incoming payload fails validation. Mule 4 replaced the exception-based model of Mule 3 with a first-class Error object and a structured error type system, making it far easier to catch, inspect, and react to specific failures instead of writing generic catch-all logic.

The Mule Error Object

Whenever a processor fails, Mule creates an Error object and attaches it to the event under error. You can reference it anywhere with error in a DataWeave expression. The object exposes several useful fields:

  • errorType — a namespaced identifier such as HTTP:NOT_FOUND or MULE:TRANSFORMATION.
  • description — a short human-readable summary.
  • detailedDescription — a longer explanation, often including the offending value.
  • cause — the underlying Java exception, useful for logging stack traces.
  • errorMessage — the Mule message (payload/attributes) at the moment of failure, which can be recovered inside a handler.

Error Type Namespaces

Every error type belongs to a namespace, most commonly MULE for core runtime errors or a connector prefix such as HTTP, DB, or VALIDATION. This lets you catch errors at exactly the granularity you need — a specific connector error, an entire namespace, or every error in the application with ANY.

Core Mule Error Types

Error TypeWhen it Occurs
MULE:TRANSFORMATIONA DataWeave transformation fails to produce the expected output.
MULE:EXPRESSIONA Mule expression cannot be evaluated.
MULE:VALIDATIONA Validation module component (e.g. is-true, is-number) fails.
MULE:CONNECTIVITYThe runtime cannot establish or maintain a connection to an external system.
MULE:RETRY_EXHAUSTEDAll configured reconnection attempts have been used up.
MULE:ROUTINGA router (Scatter-Gather, Choice) cannot route the event successfully.
MULE:SECURITYAuthentication or authorization fails.
MULE:TIMEOUTAn operation exceeds its configured timeout.
MULE:DUPLICATE_MESSAGEAn idempotent message filter detects a repeated message.
MULE:COMPOSITE_ROUTINGOne or more routes inside a Scatter-Gather fail.
MULE:UNKNOWNA Java exception is thrown that Mule cannot map to a specific error type.

Connector-Specific Errors

Connectors define their own error types layered on top of the core ones. The HTTP Requester, for example, raises HTTP:NOT_FOUND, HTTP:UNAUTHORIZED, HTTP:CONNECTIVITY, and HTTP:TIMEOUT depending on the response received. The Database connector raises DB:CONNECTIVITY or DB:QUERY_EXECUTION. Knowing these specific types lets you build precise handlers instead of swallowing every failure the same way.

<on-error-continue type="HTTP:NOT_FOUND">
    <set-payload value='{"message": "Resource not found"}' />
</on-error-continue>
<on-error-propagate type="DB:CONNECTIVITY">
    <logger level="ERROR" message="Database is unreachable: #[error.description]" />
</on-error-propagate>
Tip: You can match multiple error types in a single handler using a comma-separated list, e.g. type="HTTP:NOT_FOUND, HTTP:UNAUTHORIZED", or match an entire namespace with a wildcard like HTTP:*.

Key Points

  • Mule 4 errors are structured objects with a namespaced errorType, not opaque exceptions.
  • Core error types live under the MULE namespace; connectors add their own specific types.
  • Error type matching supports exact types, comma-separated lists, and wildcards for flexible handling.
  • The error object exposes description, cause, and the original errorMessage for debugging and recovery.

subtopics.title: On Error Continue vs On Error Propagate
subtopics.meta_description: Compare on-error-continue and on-error-propagate in Mule 4, with a comparison table, transaction behavior notes, and practical XML examples for each one.
subtopics.summary: A practical comparison of the two Mule 4 error handler types and how each affects flow execution and transactions.
subtopics.content_html:
Once you can identify an error by its type, the next decision is what the flow should do about it. Mule 4 gives you two complementary error handler components — on-error-continue and on-error-propagate — and choosing the right one determines whether a failure is quietly absorbed or bubbled up to the caller.

On Error Continue

on-error-continue treats the error as handled. After the handler's processors run, the flow resumes as if the failing component had produced whatever payload the handler leaves behind, and execution continues with the next processor after the scope that failed. This is the natural choice when you want to return a fallback response, such as a default value or a friendly error payload to an API consumer, without failing the whole request.

On Error Propagate

on-error-propagate also lets you run recovery logic (logging, notifications, cleanup) but it re-raises the error afterward. The error continues traveling up the call stack — out of the current flow and into whatever called it, whether that is a parent flow, a flow reference, or ultimately the HTTP listener, which will typically translate it into a 500-style response unless something further up catches it.

Comparison

Aspecton-error-continueon-error-propagate
Error statusMarked as handledRe-thrown after handling
Flow executionContinues after the failed scopeStops; error moves to the caller
Typical useReturn fallback/default responseFail fast, let caller or global handler decide
TransactionsCommits the transaction (unless rolled back explicitly)Rolls back the active transaction
Common locationFlow-level error handler for expected, recoverable errorsGlobal error handler for unexpected/system errors

Example

<flow name="get-customer-flow">
    <http:listener path="/customers/{id}" config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" />
    <db:select config-ref="Database_Config">
        <db:sql>SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = :id</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[{'id': attributes.uriParams.id}]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:select>
    <error-handler>
        <on-error-continue type="DB:CONNECTIVITY">
            <set-payload value='{"error": "Service temporarily unavailable"}' />
            <set-variable variableName="httpStatus" value="503" />
        </on-error-continue>
        <on-error-propagate type="MULE:VALIDATION">
            <logger level="WARN" message="Invalid customer id: #[error.description]" />
        </on-error-propagate>
    </error-handler>
</flow>

Notice that a single error-handler block can mix both strategies. Errors you know how to recover from are continued; errors that indicate a real problem the caller needs to know about are propagated, often after adding context via logging.

Note: Inside an on-error-continue, the payload and variables set by the handler become the new "current" event. Any variables set before the error occurred are still available unless explicitly overwritten.

Choosing Between the Two in API Design

In practice, most well-designed Mule APIs use both handlers together at different layers. Flow-level or Try-scope handlers close to the failing processor use on-error-continue for errors the flow genuinely knows how to recover from, such as a cache miss or an optional enrichment call that is allowed to fail silently. Anything that represents a genuine failure of the requested operation is left to propagate, ultimately reaching a global error handler that translates it into a consistent HTTP status code and error body for the API consumer. Mixing the two carelessly — for example, continuing on every error type just to avoid 500 responses — hides real problems and makes production issues much harder to diagnose, so the choice should always be driven by whether the flow can produce a genuinely correct result after the failure, not just by convenience.

Key Points

  • Use on-error-continue when the flow can produce a meaningful result despite the failure.
  • Use on-error-propagate when the caller (or a higher-level handler) needs to know the operation failed.
  • A single error handler can combine multiple on-error-continue and on-error-propagate blocks matched by error type.
  • Propagation rolls back active transactions; continue does not, unless you explicitly roll back.

subtopics.title: Try Scope
subtopics.meta_description: Understand the Mule 4 Try scope for isolating error-prone processors, attaching local error handlers, and wrapping groups of processors in local transactions.
subtopics.summary: How the Try scope isolates a group of processors with its own error handler and enables local transactions.
subtopics.content_html:
Error handlers attached directly to a flow only catch errors raised by processors in that same flow. Sometimes you need finer-grained control — the ability to wrap just a few processors and handle their failures locally without affecting the rest of the flow or forcing every processor to share one error-handling strategy. That is exactly what the Try scope is for.

What the Try Scope Does

The <try> scope, found in the Mule Core module, behaves like a mini flow: it groups a set of processors together and gives them their own dedicated error-handler. If any processor inside the Try scope fails, the surrounding flow is not affected directly — the Try scope's own handler decides whether to continue or propagate. This means you can isolate risky operations (an external API call, a database write, a file operation) from the rest of the flow's logic.

Try scopes are also the standard way to wrap a block of processors in a local transaction. By setting the transactionalAction attribute, you can make the enclosed operations (for example, several Database connector operations) commit or roll back together.

Basic Example

<flow name="process-order-flow">
    <http:listener path="/orders" config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" />
    <try>
        <db:insert config-ref="Database_Config">
            <db:sql>INSERT INTO orders (id, total) VALUES (:id, :total)</db:sql>
            <db:input-parameters>#[{'id': payload.id, 'total': payload.total}]</db:input-parameters>
        </db:insert>
        <http:request method="POST" config-ref="Notification_Config" path="/notify" />
        <error-handler>
            <on-error-continue type="HTTP:CONNECTIVITY, HTTP:TIMEOUT">
                <logger level="WARN" message="Notification failed but order was saved: #[error.description]" />
            </on-error-continue>
        </error-handler>
    </try>
    <set-payload value='{"status": "order received"}' />
</flow>

In this example, if the database insert or the notification call fails with a connectivity issue, the Try scope's local handler absorbs it and logs a warning, while the flow still returns a success response. Without the Try scope, an unhandled failure in the notification call would abort the whole flow.

Transactional Try Scopes

<try transactionalAction="ALWAYS_BEGIN">
    <db:insert config-ref="Database_Config">
        <db:sql>INSERT INTO accounts (id, balance) VALUES (:id, :balance)</db:sql>
    </db:insert>
    <db:update config-ref="Database_Config">
        <db:sql>UPDATE ledger SET total = total + :balance WHERE account_id = :id</db:sql>
    </db:update>
</try>

With ALWAYS_BEGIN, Mule starts a new local transaction for the enclosed operations. If any operation fails and the error is not explicitly continued, the transaction rolls back automatically, keeping the database consistent.

Try Scope vs Flow-Level Error Handler

AspectTry ScopeFlow-Level Error Handler
Scope of protectionOnly processors inside the <try> blockEvery processor in the flow
ReusabilityCan be repeated with different strategies within one flowOne handler per flow
TransactionsSupports transactionalAction directlyNot transaction-scoped by itself
Tip: Use Try scopes to isolate non-critical side effects (notifications, logging, analytics calls) so their failure never blocks the primary business outcome of a flow.

Key Points

  • Try scope wraps a subset of processors with their own local error handler.
  • Errors inside a Try scope do not automatically propagate to the parent flow.
  • Try scopes are the standard mechanism for local transactions in Mule 4.
  • Use Try scopes to isolate risky or non-essential operations from critical flow logic.

subtopics.title: Global Error Handler
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how to define a reusable global error-handler in Mule 4, reference it from individual flows, and configure it as the application-wide default handler.
subtopics.summary: How to centralize error-handling logic in a global error handler and apply it across every flow in an application.
subtopics.content_html:
Repeating the same error-handling logic in every flow of a large Mule application quickly becomes unmaintainable. Mule 4 solves this with a global error handler: a reusable, top-level error-handler configuration that any number of flows can reference, or that can be set as the default handler for the whole application.

Defining a Global Error Handler

A global error handler is declared outside of any flow, typically in global.xml or at the top of your main configuration file, using the same on-error-continue and on-error-propagate building blocks you would use locally.

<error-handler name="global-error-handler">
    <on-error-propagate type="HTTP:NOT_FOUND">
        <set-payload value='{"error": "Not Found", "message": error.description}' />
        <set-variable variableName="httpStatus" value="404" />
    </on-error-propagate>
    <on-error-propagate type="MULE:VALIDATION, APIKIT:BAD_REQUEST">
        <set-payload value='{"error": "Bad Request", "message": error.description}' />
        <set-variable variableName="httpStatus" value="400" />
    </on-error-propagate>
    <on-error-propagate type="ANY">
        <logger level="ERROR" message="Unhandled error: #[error.description] - #[error.detailedDescription]" />
        <set-payload value='{"error": "Internal Server Error"}' />
        <set-variable variableName="httpStatus" value="500" />
    </on-error-propagate>
</error-handler>

Order matters: Mule evaluates the blocks top to bottom and stops at the first one whose type matches, so list more specific error types before generic ones like ANY.

Referencing It From a Flow

Any flow can point to the global handler by name using the ref attribute instead of defining an inline handler:

<flow name="get-orders-flow">
    <http:listener path="/orders" config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" />
    <flow-ref name="fetch-orders-subflow" />
    <error-handler ref="global-error-handler" />
</flow>

Setting a Default Error Handler

Rather than adding error-handler ref="..." to every flow, you can configure a global handler as the application-wide default inside the Configuration element:

<configuration defaultErrorHandler-ref="global-error-handler" />

With this in place, every flow that does not define its own error handler automatically falls back to the global one. Flows that need special behavior can still declare a local error-handler, which takes precedence.

Combining Global and Local Handling

A common, robust pattern is to use local on-error-continue blocks (or Try scopes) for errors a flow can gracefully recover from, and let everything else propagate up to the global handler, which is responsible for consistent HTTP status codes and error payload shapes across the entire API.

Note: Global error handlers are especially valuable in APIkit-based projects, where consistent error response formatting across dozens of resource/method combinations is essential for a well-behaved REST API.

Organizing Global Error Handlers Across Modules

In larger projects it is common to split error handling into more than one reusable handler — for example, one for the public-facing API layer that maps errors to REST-friendly JSON payloads, and another for internal system/process layer flows where errors are logged and re-thrown without shaping an HTTP response at all. Both can live in a shared configuration file that is imported into every module, keeping the mapping between error types and observable behavior in one place instead of scattered across dozens of flow files. This also makes it much easier to update error formatting later: a single change to the global handler automatically applies everywhere it is referenced, rather than requiring an update to every flow individually.

Key Points

  • A global error-handler centralizes error-handling logic so it isn't duplicated per flow.
  • Flows opt in with error-handler ref="name", or you can set one as the application default via defaultErrorHandler-ref.
  • Order error blocks from most specific to most general; the first match wins.
  • Global handlers are the standard place to normalize HTTP status codes and error response bodies for APIs.

subtopics.title: Custom Error Types and Reconnection Strategies
subtopics.meta_description: Raise custom business error types with raise-error and configure reconnect and reconnect-forever strategies in Mule 4 for building resilient integrations.
subtopics.summary: How to model business failures with custom error types and configure connector reconnection strategies for resilience.
subtopics.content_html:
Built-in and connector error types cover infrastructure-level failures, but real applications also need to signal business-level problems — an order that fails validation against custom rules, or a customer record that violates a business constraint. Mule 4 lets you define and raise your own error types, and it provides configurable reconnection strategies to make integrations more resilient to transient failures.

Declaring Custom Error Types

A flow can declare the custom errors it is able to raise using the <raise-error> component together with an errors section in the flow, which documents the errorType and lets Mule validate it at design time.

<flow name="validate-order-flow">
    <raise-error type="APP:INVALID_ORDER" description="Order total must be greater than zero" />
</flow>

Custom error types conventionally use a namespace such as APP (your application's own namespace) followed by an identifier in upper snake case, e.g. APP:INVALID_ORDER, APP:DUPLICATE_CUSTOMER, or APP:INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS. You can then catch these exactly like built-in errors:

<on-error-propagate type="APP:INVALID_ORDER">
    <set-payload value='{"error": "InvalidOrder", "message": error.description}' />
    <set-variable variableName="httpStatus" value="422" />
</on-error-propagate>

Raising Errors Conditionally

Combine <raise-error> with a Validation module component or a Choice router to enforce business rules explicitly:

<choice>
    <when expression="#[payload.total <= 0]">
        <raise-error type="APP:INVALID_ORDER" description="Order total must be positive" />
    </when>
    <otherwise>
        <flow-ref name="save-order-subflow" />
    </otherwise>
</choice>

Reconnection Strategies

Many connectivity failures — a database restarting, a brief network blip — are transient and resolve themselves quickly. Rather than failing immediately, most connectors support a reconnection strategy configured on the connector's global configuration element.

<db:config name="Database_Config">
    <db:my-sql-connection host="${db.host}" port="${db.port}" user="${db.user}" password="${db.password}">
        <reconnection>
            <reconnect frequency="3000" count="5" />
        </reconnection>
    </db:my-sql-connection>
</db:config>

Two strategies are available:

  • reconnect — retries a fixed number of times (count) at a fixed interval (frequency, in milliseconds), then gives up and raises MULE:RETRY_EXHAUSTED.
  • reconnect-forever — keeps retrying indefinitely at the given frequency, useful for background pollers where you never want to stop trying to reconnect.
<reconnection>
    <reconnect-forever frequency="5000" />
</reconnection>

Handling Retry Exhaustion

When a fixed reconnect strategy runs out of attempts, Mule raises MULE:RETRY_EXHAUSTED, which you can catch in an error handler to alert operations or fail gracefully:

<on-error-propagate type="MULE:RETRY_EXHAUSTED">
    <logger level="ERROR" message="Connection retries exhausted: #[error.description]" />
</on-error-propagate>
Tip: Combine reconnection strategies at the connector level with an Until Successful scope around a broader block of logic when you need retry behavior that spans more than a single connector operation.

Custom Errors and API Consumers

Custom error types are most valuable when they are mapped to meaningful HTTP status codes and clear messages in your global error handler, so API consumers receive something actionable instead of a generic 500 response. A well-designed set of application errors — APP:INVALID_ORDER mapped to 422, APP:DUPLICATE_CUSTOMER mapped to 409, APP:INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS mapped to 402 — effectively becomes part of your API's public contract, and it is worth documenting these custom error types in your RAML or OAS specification's response definitions so consumers know what to expect and can build their own retry or fallback logic accordingly.

Key Points

  • Custom error types let you model business failures with the same error-handling tools as system errors.
  • <raise-error> raises a custom or built-in error type with a description you control.
  • reconnect retries a bounded number of times; reconnect-forever retries indefinitely.
  • Exhausted retries surface as MULE:RETRY_EXHAUSTED, which should be handled explicitly at the boundary of the application.
